findings.claim: most chapters end with a practical decision context (compliance versus accommodation; legal minimum versus ethical maximum; short-term profit versus long-term goodwill)
findings.failure_mode: Placement wrong and not in the deep ref: the source's 'What Would You Do?' and 'Cases from the Real World' features sit throughout chapters, not at their ends; the three parenthetical contexts are the distillation's characterisation.
findings.evidence: Deep ref carries no description of the feature boxes. Source 370-384 (Preface: 'Throughout Business Ethics, you will find features...'; 'What Would You Do? This feature presents brief, fact-based scenarios in which students are challenged to put themselves into the shoes of ranking executives and balance a host of interests').
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to the Structure line: the Preface's 'What Would You Do?' feature "presents brief, fact-based scenarios in which students are challenged to put themselves into the shoes of ranking executives and balance a host of interests—some conflicting—as they make decisions for their businesses" [V] (Preface); then correct: its 'What Would You Do?' features set practical decision scenarios throughout the chapters.

findings.claim: Second, the *moral minimum* (legal compliance) is rarely sufficient
findings.failure_mode: Copies a deep-ref error. The source defines the moral minimum as honouring obligations to all stakeholders, and calls legal compliance the ethical minimum; the distillation's own Key Concept 4 and What-to-Look-For pattern 1 draw that distinction correctly, so line 10 contradicts them.
findings.evidence: Deep 19 ('the moral minimum — legal compliance — is rarely sufficient') vs deep 146 (moral minimum = honouring obligations to all stakeholders). Source 5343-5345 (moral minimum); source 3870 ('An ethical minimum, or the least a company might do that complies with the law').
findings.fix: correct: Second, legal compliance (the ethical minimum) is rarely sufficient; ethical maximums protect long-term profitability and reputation more reliably. Also cycle-to-deep: fix deep line 19 to read 'the ethical minimum — legal compliance — is rarely sufficient'.

findings.claim: "tacit knowledge acquired from experience that enables people to make prudent judgments ... guided by values and morals" [V]
findings.failure_mode: Marker incomplete: these are Nonaka and Takeuchi's words quoted by the source (the distillation's own note at line 180 lists phronesis as [BT]).
findings.evidence: Source 897-900 ('The authors conclude that "...Practical wisdom is tacit knowledge acquired from experience..."'); deep 35 (citing Nonaka and Takeuchi).
findings.fix: re-mark: [V] [BT]

findings.claim: The single-standard reasoning protects against hypocrisy, builds reputation, and reduces decision overhead.
findings.failure_mode: Supported by the source's Ch 1.3 argument (inconsistency harms reputation; stakeholders recognise hypocrisy; a single standard makes consistent behaviour easier), none of which the deep ref carries.
findings.evidence: Deep 51-57 (no benefits listed). Source 1275-1276 ('lack a consistent ethical core, which can harm our reputation'); 1342-1345 ('Stakeholders recognize such hypocrisy'); 1270 ('a single ethical standard makes behaving consistently easier'); 1318-1324.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to the Ch 1.3 paragraph: inconsistent standards mean our conduct "lack[s] a consistent ethical core, which can harm our reputation and that of the business" and "Stakeholders recognize such hypocrisy and rightly hold it against the business's leaders" [V] (Ch 1.3, "Multiple versus Single Ethical Standards"); then correct: The source argues a single standard guards against visible hypocrisy, protects reputation, and makes consistent behaviour easier.

findings.claim: *Ethical minimum* is the least a company might do that complies with the law.
findings.failure_mode: Definition taken from the source's in-text Samsung passage; the deep ref carries only the key-term definition ('the least a company might do to claim it holds an ethically positive position').
findings.evidence: Deep 107. Source 3870 ('An ethical minimum, or the least a company might do that complies with the law, would have been to offer the warning and nothing more').
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 107: "An ethical minimum, or the least a company might do that complies with the law, would have been to offer the warning and nothing more" [V] (Ch 3.1, "Ethical Responsibilities Often Extend Beyond Legal Requirements").

findings.claim: Kant: "Act only according to that maxim whereby you can, at the same time, will that it should become a universal law" [V]
findings.failure_mode: Marker incomplete: Kant's words relayed by the source; the distillation's own note (line 179) lists Kant as [BT].
findings.evidence: Deep 89 and 522 ('citing Kant, categorical imperative').
findings.fix: re-mark: [V] [BT]

findings.claim: Mill's harm-principle quotation marked [V]
findings.failure_mode: Marker incomplete: Mill's words relayed by the source; the distillation's own note (line 178) lists Mill as [BT].
findings.evidence: Deep 85 and 518 ('citing Mill, On Liberty').
findings.fix: re-mark: [V] [BT]

findings.claim: goodwill, brand, employee retention, customer loyalty are slow-built and slow-eroded
findings.failure_mode: The deep ref says goodwill cannot be earned in a short time, but also that negative employee actions on social media damage brands swiftly; the source adds that the companies suffered 'financial and goodwill losses' from single incidents. Slow to build, fast to lose.
findings.evidence: Deep 41 ('Goodwill cannot be earned in a short time'); deep 280 ('Negative employee actions on social media damage brands swiftly'). Source 10825-10827.
findings.fix: correct: goodwill, brand, employee commitment and customer loyalty are slow to build (Ch 1.2) and can be damaged quickly (Ch 7.2, "Respecting the Brand").

findings.claim: Employees often rationalise unethical conduct as sanctioned by superiors — abdicating personal responsibility.
findings.failure_mode: Supported by the source but not carried by the deep ref, which says only 'Bias diminishes moral agency'; 'often' also loosens the source's 'An example of bias occurs when...'.
findings.evidence: Deep 204. Source 8229-8232 ('An example of bias occurs when employees engage in unethical activity because it has been sanctioned by higher-ups. They abdicate personal responsibility by assigning blame elsewhere').
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 204: "An example of bias occurs when employees engage in unethical activity because it has been sanctioned by higher-ups. They abdicate personal responsibility by assigning blame elsewhere" [V] (Ch 5.4, "Normative Business Ethics"); then correct: One bias the source names: employees acting unethically because higher-ups sanctioned it, abdicating personal responsibility.

findings.claim: "Facilitating payments" are a narrow exception.
findings.failure_mode: Supported by the source but absent from the deep ref; the source's exception is narrower than stated and bears directly on the worked example (small payments to low-level workers for routine tasks, 'but not to influence the granting of a contract').
findings.evidence: Deep 298 (no exception mentioned). Source 11410-11412.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 298: An exception is made for "facilitating or grease payments," small amounts of money paid to low-level government workers in an effort to speed routine tasks like processing paperwork or turning on electricity, but not to influence the granting of a contract [V] (Ch 7.4, "Bribery and the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act").

findings.claim: The Bill Swanson plagiarism case illustrates the inverse: top-down ethical claims undermined by personal failure compromise organisational ethics.
findings.failure_mode: Effect overstated: the deep ref reports the booklet discontinued and retirement package reduced; the source says the greatest damage was to his reputation. Neither says organisational ethics were compromised.
findings.evidence: Deep 472. Source 18002-18006 ('the greatest damage was to his reputation, despite an otherwise distinguished 42-year career').
findings.fix: correct: The Bill Swanson plagiarism case (Ch 11.3, "Swanson's Rule #1: Don't Plagiarize") shows the cost to a leader whose published ethical maxims proved plagiarised: the booklet was discontinued and his retirement package reduced.

findings.claim: Is this decision preventing harm to others, or limiting choice for the actor's own good? The latter requires special justification.
findings.failure_mode: Loosened: Mill says the actor's own good 'is not a sufficient warrant', not that it needs special justification.
findings.evidence: Deep 85 ('His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant').
findings.fix: correct: The latter, on Mill's principle, is not a sufficient warrant for exercising power over someone against their will.

findings.claim: Stakeholders accept difficult decisions more readily when the reasoning is shared.
findings.failure_mode: Stated as a general finding; the deep ref does not carry it. The source's closest support is narrower: a transparency duty to employees, with fuller understanding 'usually' giving a better working relationship, especially around layoffs.
findings.evidence: Deep ref: nothing on sharing reasoning. Source 8675-8681 ('A more complete understanding of all relevant information usually results in a better working relationship'); 8690-8692 (transparency in layoffs and closings).
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to Ch 6.1: the duty of transparency to the workforce, "A more complete understanding of all relevant information usually results in a better working relationship" [V] (Ch 6.1); then correct: The source holds that a company owes employees transparency about significant matters that affect them, especially layoffs and closings (Ch 6.1).

findings.claim: The career-cost data on whistleblowers is sobering even when their action was unambiguously ethical.
findings.failure_mode: The source gives cases (Watkins, Krawcheck) and qualitative risks, not data on whistleblower career costs.
findings.evidence: Deep 312-314 (Watkins, Krawcheck cases). No career-cost statistics in the deep ref.
findings.fix: correct: The career costs in the source's cases (Watkins at Enron, Krawcheck at Merrill Lynch) are sobering even when the action was unambiguously ethical (Ch 7.5).

findings.claim: Review whether escalation of commitment is operating ... Is the sunk cost being treated as recoverable?
findings.failure_mode: Concept not in this source's deep ref; it belongs to OpenStax Organizational Behavior (Ch 6.4, six barriers). Unattributed here, it reads as Business Ethics content.
findings.evidence: Business Ethics deep: no escalation of commitment. OB deep 186 ('Escalation of commitment: decision-makers stay committed to poor decisions even as costs mount', Ch 6.4).
findings.fix: correct: append '(see OpenStax Organizational Behavior, Ch 6.4, "escalation of commitment")' or move the row to the OB distillation.

findings.claim: Stakeholder claims weighed by power alone ... Diagnosis: the prioritisation is descriptive without the normative lens (Donaldson and Preston).
findings.failure_mode: Mislabelled approach: the descriptive approach aims to model stakeholder interests accurately and balance them as fairly as possible; weighing by power alone is not what it describes. Treating stakeholders as means to outcomes is the instrumental approach.
findings.evidence: Deep 111 (descriptive: 'develop the most accurate model and balance interests fairly'; instrumental: connects stakeholder management to financial outcomes). Source 4004-4006.
findings.fix: correct: Diagnosis: stakeholders are being treated instrumentally, as means to outcomes, without the normative lens (Donaldson and Preston).

findings.claim: the 30% benefits saving is "the margin between middle class and below"
findings.failure_mode: Quotation not verbatim.
findings.evidence: Deep 354: 'is often the margin between being in the middle class and falling below it'. Source 13247-13248.
findings.fix: correct: the 30 percent saving "is often the margin between being in the middle class and falling below it" [V] (Ch 8.4)

findings.claim: securing a key government contract will require a "facilitation payment" ... The director declines the facilitation payment (line 144)
findings.failure_mode: Concept misapplied: on the source's terms a payment to influence the granting of a contract is not a facilitating payment at all, so the example adopts the CFO's label without naming the distinction its own Key Concept 11 raises.
findings.evidence: Source 11410-11412 (exception covers small payments to low-level workers for routine tasks, 'but not to influence the granting of a contract'); not in deep (see D010).
findings.fix: correct: add to 'Recognising the ethical dimension': The label is wrong on the source's terms: the FCPA's exception covers only small "facilitating or grease payments" to low-level workers to speed routine tasks, "but not to influence the granting of a contract" (Ch 7.4). This is a bribe. (And at line 144: 'The director declines the payment.')

findings.claim: the FCPA framework is built precisely to deny the cultural-relativism defence (also line 142: 'exactly the failure mode the FCPA was designed to address')
findings.failure_mode: Attributes a design purpose to the FCPA that the deep ref does not give; the deep ref carries the book's own rejection of the relativism defence and its endorsement of the FCPA position.
findings.evidence: Deep 15 (book rejects 'when in Rome' defence of bribery); deep 298 (FCPA prohibits bribery of foreign officials); deep 647.
findings.fix: correct: the book rejects the "when in Rome" defence of bribery and endorses the FCPA's prohibition (Ch 1.3, Ch 7.4).

findings.claim: Cultural relativism used to justify bribery, sweatshops, environmental dumping. The single-standard rule rejects this defence.
findings.failure_mode: 'Environmental dumping' is not among the deep ref's relativism cases (bribery, kickbacks, sweatshops, corruption); the source does raise it (toxic waste dumped in countries that allow it). Same addition at line 124.
findings.evidence: Deep 15. Source 6005-6009 ('Is It Ethical to Dump Toxic Waste in Countries That Allow It?').
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to Ch 5: the source's box "Is It Ethical to Dump Toxic Waste in Countries That Allow It?" asking whether a multinational should "take advantage of another country's lack of regulation or enforcement if it saves money to do so" [V] (Ch 5).

findings.claim: the False Claims Act and protected disclosure statutes exist precisely because internal channels often fail
findings.failure_mode: The source gives a different reason for the FCA: Congress feared Civil War suppliers would cheat the government. No statute's purpose is tied to failing internal channels; the source advises trying internal channels first.
findings.evidence: Deep 308 (try internal channels first), deep 310 (FCA passed during the Civil War). Source 11722-11723 ('enacted in 1863, during the American Civil War, because Congress was worried that suppliers of goods to the Union Army might cheat the government').
findings.fix: correct: "Whistleblowers are disloyal." Treating ethical dissent as betrayal; the source advises internal channels first, protects external reporting through more than twenty federal statutes, and shows what speaking up cost Watkins and Krawcheck (Ch 7.5).

findings.claim: *Samsung washer recall* — cited as a paradigmatic ethical-maximum response (Ch 4.1) [BT].
findings.failure_mode: Wrong chapter and marker: the case is in Ch 3.1 (as Key Concept 4 correctly cites) and is the textbook's own example, not a borrowed-through authority.
findings.evidence: Deep 107 (Samsung washer recall, Ch 3.1).
findings.fix: correct: *Samsung washer recall* — the source's own example of an ethical-maximum response (Ch 3.1) [AE].

findings.claim: The worked example's enforcement figures (BHP Billiton, GlaxoSmithKline, Telia) trace to `[BT]` passages in the deep ref
findings.failure_mode: The deep ref carries these figures unmarked as the textbook's own reporting (Ch 7.4), not as [BT].
findings.evidence: Deep 298 (BHP Billiton, GSK $25 million; Telia $965 million; no marker).
findings.fix: correct: The worked example's enforcement figures (BHP Billiton, GlaxoSmithKline, Telia) trace to the deep ref's Ch 7.4 passage and should be independently verified before use in a live compliance context.

findings.claim: Six months later, news emerges that the competitor is under DOJ investigation ... The director files this as a phronesis lesson: ... the deontological line settled the matter and the long-term consequences vindicated it.
findings.failure_mode: Invented outcome framed as the framework's payoff ('vindicated'); the deep ref reports the book's argument, not results. It also cuts against the distillation's own Phase 6 point that outcomes do not grade decisions.
findings.evidence: Deep 19, 484 (argument only); distillation line 101.
findings.fix: correct: The director files this as a phronesis lesson: the consequence-only calculation the CFO offered was incomplete, and the deontological line settled the matter whatever the outcome.

notes: Most substance traces. Two CONTRADICTED: 'slow-eroded' goodwill (deep 280 says brand damage is swift) and the claim that whistleblower statutes exist because internal channels fail (source gives the FCA's Civil War procurement-fraud reason). Line 10 copies a deep-ref error at deep line 19 (moral minimum = legal compliance), which the source and deep 146 contradict; the deep should be fixed. Several claims lean on source passages the deep ref lacks (ethical minimum = legal compliance, facilitating-payment exception, abdicating responsibility, single-standard benefits, environmental dumping): cycle them to the deep. Third-party quotations (Kant, Mill, Nonaka-Takeuchi) carry [V] only while the distillation's own notes call them [BT]. The worked example's closing DOJ vindication is graded MINOR-DRIFT for consistency with the other distillations' invented payoffs. Integration claims about OB (reflective/reactive, six barriers, escalation of commitment, groupthink, six-step process, Rest's four components) check out against the OB deep ref.
